questions.question: What does map return?
options: A new array of the same length
Only the elements that pass a test
questions.explanation: The callback return values become the new elements.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke
reference.excerpt: The map method transforms an array by applying a function to all of its elements and building a new array from the returned values.

questions.question: What does forEach return?
options: A new array of callback results
questions.explanation: forEach is for side effects. The callback return is ignored.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: None of the methods described here modify the array on which they are invoked

questions.question: ["10", "10", "10"].map(parseInt) is…
questions.explanation: map passes the index as parseInt's radix. Use Number, or (s) => parseInt(s, 10).

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke
reference.excerpt: The map method transforms an array by applying a function to all of its elements and building a new array from the returned values.

questions.question: filter compared with deleting inside a loop…
options: Removes elements from the same array
Builds a new array and leaves the original
Throws if the predicate is false
questions.explanation: The book version pushes keepers into a fresh array.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke
reference.excerpt: Note how the filter function, rather than deleting elements from the existing array, builds up a new array with only the elements that pass

questions.question: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1].filter((x) => x < 3) is…
questions.explanation: Order of survivors is preserved. It does not sort them.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: a.filter(x => x < 3)         // => [2, 1]; values less than 3

questions.question: reduce([1, 2, 3, 4], (a, b) => a + b, 0) is…
questions.explanation: Start at 0, then add each element.

reference.book: Eloquent JavaScript, 4th Edition by Marijn Haverbeke
reference.excerpt: The parameters to reduce are, apart from the array, a combining function and a start value.

questions.question: [].reduce((a, b) => a + b) does what?
questions.explanation: No start value and no first element. Pass 0 if the array might be empty.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: Calling reduce() on an empty array with no initial value argument causes a TypeError.

questions.question: [7].reduce((a, b) => a + b) with no start value…
options: Throws, because the callback needs two numbers
Returns 7 and does not call the callback
questions.explanation: One element and no initial value: that element is the result.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: If you call it with only one value—either an array with one element and no initial value or an empty array and an initial value—it simply returns that one value without ever calling the reduction function.

questions.question: some and every stop early when…
questions.explanation: some returns on the first truthy predicate. every returns on the first falsy one.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: Note that both every() and some() stop iterating array elements as soon as they know what value to return.

questions.question: every([]) is…
questions.explanation: There is no element that fails the test. some([]) is false.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: Note that both every() and some() stop iterating array elements as soon as they know what value to return.

questions.question: slice(1, 3) on [1, 2, 3, 4]…
options: Mutates the array to [1, 4] and returns [2, 3]
questions.explanation: End is exclusive. slice copies.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: The slice() method returns a slice, or subarray, of the specified array.

questions.question: splice(1, 2) on [1, 2, 3, 4] returns…
questions.explanation: The array itself becomes [1, 4]. The return value is what was removed.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan

questions.question: [33, 4, 1111, 222].sort() with no comparator is…
questions.explanation: Default sort compares strings. "1111" comes before "4".

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: a.sort();               // a == [1111, 222, 33, 4]; alphabetical order

questions.question: A numeric sort comparator (a, b) => a - b means…
options: Negative puts a first, positive puts b first
The original array is copied first
questions.explanation: sort still mutates. Copy with slice if you need the old order.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: a.sort((a,b) => b-a);   // a == [1111, 222, 33, 4]; reverse numerical order

questions.question: find when nothing matches returns…
questions.explanation: findIndex returns -1. find returns undefined.

questions.question: [1, [2, [3]]].flat() is…

questions.question: Which chain leaves the source array unchanged?

questions.question: Why is a hole in a sparse array different under filter than under map?
options: filter calls the predicate on the hole
map keeps the hole; filter skips holes and returns a dense array
questions.explanation: Flanagan: filter skips missing elements and the result is always dense.

reference.book: JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, 7th Edition by David Flanagan
reference.excerpt: Note that filter() skips missing elements in sparse arrays and that its return value is always dense.
